query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy, service‐relevant thermal and mechanical loading can trigger incipient solute segregation that nucleates nanoscale, ordered (brittle) precipitates along internal interfaces (e.g. grain or phase boundaries), thereby locally reducing toughness and promoting brittle crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase high‐entropy alloy with a uniform, disordered solid solution microstructure that has not yet shown detectable precipitates or grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Expose otherwise identical alloy samples to controlled thermal aging (or cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperatures) that mimics service conditions.
generation.conditions: Temperatures and stresses representative of demanding engineering applications, where holding times or cyclic loads are sufficient to allow subtle solute clustering (e.g. moderate temperature aging for several hours/days or in‐service stress cycles).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale ordered precipitates (e.g. B2 or similar intermetallic phases) forming preferentially at grain boundaries or interfacial regions due to local solute segregation.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation or stress promotes local rearrangements within the high internal entropy matrix, leading to subtle compositional fluctuations. These fluctuations enable the nucleation of ordered, brittle phases at internal interfaces that, despite the overall single‐phase appearance, create localized stress concentrators and facilitate intergranular crack propagation, thus degrading toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to as-cast samples, aged or cyclically loaded samples will exhibit a measurable drop in toughness (via lower impact energy or fracture toughness) coinciding with microstructural evidence (via TEM/SEM) of nanoscale, ordered precipitate formation at internal interfaces.
generation.baseline: The initial toughness and homogeneous microstructure of the as-cast single-phase high-entropy alloy with no detectable segregation.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under service conditions that involve moderate to high temperatures and sustained or cyclic mechanical loading; at very low temperatures or under very rapid loading, the incipient phase decomposition may not have time to develop.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature (phase type, size, distribution) and kinetics of the precipitate formation may vary with precise alloy composition and loading history. Additionally, other concurrent deformation mechanisms might mask or interact with the embrittlement process, complicating the quantitative prediction of toughness loss.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical as-cast single-phase high-entropy alloy specimens. Subject one set to a controlled thermal aging treatment (or cyclic mechanical loading at elevated temperature) meant to simulate service conditions, while keeping the other set as an untreated control. Perform detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM and high-resolution SEM) to detect any development of nanoscale ordered precipitates, especially at grain boundaries. Conduct standardized toughness tests (e.g., impact or fracture toughness measurements) on both sets to compare their mechanical performance.
measurements: Grain boundary and intra-granular microstructural characterization via TEM/SEM
Phase analysis (e.g., XRD) to detect any additional ordering or new phase formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show any statistically significant drop in toughness compared to the control and no evidence of nanoscale, ordered precipitate formation or solute segregation is found at internal interfaces, then the hypothesis that service loading promotes embrittlement through incipient phase decomposition is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
